modo: T180: LAB -- head jitter root-caused to a 0.8 s stale dead-reckoning anchor: Basalt's input queue was a latency reservoir; bounded it and the delivered pose noise collapsed 20x
driver: lab-full + basalt 0002 (76d71a8), jack-in-wayland.sh 1 6dof, headset motionless on the desk the whole time, hello_xr as pose querent, static A/B/C/D/E ladder
veredicto: THE HEAD'S REMAINING JITTER IS POSITIONAL AND IT WAS BORN IN A QUEUE. Baseline (constellation on, threads 2, 915 s static): raw SLAM at rest is excellent -- rot step p99 0.15 deg, pos residual p50 0.27 mm / p90 0.86 mm -- but the pose the app receives wanders p50 4.1 / p90 11.5 mm, and with constellation off it got WORSE (9.8/24.6 mm): the output path was adding an order of magnitude over raw. NOT the filter, NOT prediction per se: timing.csv's second-minus-first column read p50 852 ms -- the SLAM pose Monado anchors dead reckoning to was almost a second old, permanently, so predict integrated accel noise over 0.85 s. Mechanism, read from the source after enforce_realtime measurably did nothing: Basalt's input_img_queue (capacity 10) sits permanently full when the optical flow (~26 fps max at any thread count; 55-60 ms/frame serial at 2 threads) is slower than the camera (30 fps): 380 ms parked right there, push_frame's BLOCKING push back-pressures Monado into dropping ~half the frames blindly at its own door (16.3 Hz pose rate), and vio_enforce_realtime drops in the VIO stage, DOWNSTREAM of the jam -- measured: zero effect on rate or backlog. NOT CPU starvation: constellation off freed ~3 cores (5.5 -> 2) and the rate stayed 17-18 Hz. BASALT 0002: cap input_img_queue at 2, push-the-newest-drop-the-oldest in push_frame (the policy the same file already used for monado_out_state_queue), deterministic mode untouched. Measured, same rig same config: frame->pose age p50 819 -> 109 ms; delivered position residual at rest p50 9.8 -> 0.57 mm, p90 24.6 -> 1.23 mm, p99 39.9 -> 2.2 mm; delivered rot residual p99 0.146 -> 0.107 deg; raw itself improved (pos step p99 2.3 -> 1.4 mm) because frames now arrive fresh and evenly spaced. SLAM_THREADS 2->4 lifts throughput 17.3 -> 25.9 Hz (idle, constellation off); launcher default stays 2 until the in-game side is re-measured -- with 0002 in, threads buy pose rate, not freshness. WEARER VERDICT PENDING: every number here is static-on-desk; the physical rule stands. TOOLING: scripts/head-jitter.py (static windows, raw vs delivered, jitter split from drift) + docs/32 rows, including two new blindness entries -- pose-lag.py is blind to wall-clock delivery delay (both CSVs carry frame timestamps, so a pose 0.85 s late cross-correlates at ~0 lag: it read 'delivered leads raw by 5 ms' while the tracker ran 0.8 s behind, both true), and filtering.csv is EMPTY without a querent (no client connected -> nothing calls predict/filter; cost one confused measurement). Also: filtering.csv interleaves querents (compositor ~90 Hz future timestamps + constellation tracker at past camera timestamps + implausible-clock rows) -- clean to the strictly-monotonic in-session subsequence before computing anything, the raw file shows 135 deg / kilometre 'steps' that are pure interleaving artefacts. CONTROLLERS PREP (not run): wmr_controller_base.c's gravity measurement now also logs the disagreement via P_imu_me (via_P_imu_me=), built and ready; prediction is the 104-deg low mode collapses toward 0 while the wrong lobe keeps ~161. Blocked on: controllers never registered this boot (left/right None -- asleep after an hour static, T043 no-hot-add) and the USB2 branch flapped 3/5 -> 4/5 -> 5/5 -> 3/5 across three service restarts (the known marginal-contact storm; docs/22).

modo: T181: LAB -- the constellation's tie-breaker exists and is measured, but it is NOT the factory transform: the bridge is the WMR axes flip, found by waving the controllers
driver: lab-full 63b5317c8 (0001-0047), jack-in-wayland.sh 1 6dof + constellation, both controllers static at ~40cm then waved 90s, user working the hardware
veredicto: THE 0046 HYPOTHESIS DIED AND SOMETHING BETTER REPLACED IT. Plan was: apply sensors.accel.pose (P_imu_me, 105.3/105.5 deg mirrored) and watch the constellation-vs-IMU gravity disagreement collapse for true solves. Measured (5 min static, both hands, telemetry extended to log raw quaternions): NO composition of P, conj(P), or any axis-fix conjugation collapses both hands at once -- the left's raw disagreement was already low (20 deg) and P made it WORSE (65), the right went 140->110. Static data is underdetermined here: two unknown fixed rotations (body bridge + possible world-convention mismatch) plus a per-session fusion yaw. Each bistability lobe IS rigid to 1-3 deg though (delta clustering, 4 lobes left / 1 lobe right that window), so a constant bridge exists. THE IDENTIFICATION THAT WORKED BYPASSES WORLDS ENTIRELY: the user waved both controllers 90 s and Wahba over paired relative rotations (same physical rotation, two body frames; rotation-angle agreement p50 0.4-0.5 deg validates rigidity) gave 178.9 deg about X (left) and 178.8 (right) -- Rx180, the WMR y/z axes-swap convention wmr_hmd.c already corrects for the HMD, identical on both hands as a convention must be. The 105-deg-equals-low-mode match that closed T179 was a COINCIDENCE. Also fixed a conceptual bug in the inherited metric: rotating body -y into world is NOT yaw-immune as its 2026-08-12 comment claimed; world-down expressed in the body frame is. PATCH 0047, the gravity gate: candidate solves whose body-frame world-down disagrees with the fusion's through Rx180 by more than WMR_CONSTELLATION_GRAVITY_GATE_DEG (default 14; true lobes p90 4.3/6.5, flip ghosts p50 21 p90 89) are dropped before entering the relation history, so the tracker's own prior stays on the true lobe; gated only while IMU data flows so it cannot block initial lock. VALIDATED STATIC, LIVE: every sampled drop was a 105-128 deg flip, every accepted sample under 7 deg, ~1.7 drops/s while static. WHAT SURVIVES THE GATE, measured immediately and by construction: near-pure-yaw mis-assignments keep gravity intact -- the right controller still alternates between 3 stable position clusters 20-30 cm apart, each at 0.07-0.08 px. The hands-jump problem is now HALVED (orientation flips dead, the 0.41-0.44 m healthy-metrics class), and the remaining open problem is precise: feed the position/orientation prior into the solver's assignment search, or disambiguate pattern phase. In-game wearer verdict pending (Propagation VR). HARDWARE FRICTION, all night: the controllers POWER OFF after ~15 min of stillness (bit three times -- garbage near-origin solves at 1.4-1.7 px on ambient IR blobs are the LEDs-off signature; the gate correctly kills those too); re-attach of an already-registered controller after mid-session power-on WORKS without a service restart, twice observed -- nuance to T043's no-hot-add (which is about unregistered devices at startup); the USB2 branch flapped 5/5->3/5->4/5->5/5->3/5->5/5 across the night's restarts with a 55k-line companion os_hid_read -1 storm mid-session (docs/22 marginal contact; the controller tunnel is on the USB3 HoloLens device per docs/03, so tracking survived it). A WRONG TURN KEPT HONEST: one session ran with WMR_LOG=debug and its per-blob spam, a dead companion AND (unknowingly) sleeping controllers -- the solve collapse seen there was attributed to nothing, deliberately, and the telemetry line moved to INFO so reading it never requires the debug firehose again. TOOLS: scripts/constellation-frame-fit.py (the Wahba identification), scripts/constellation-gate-validate.py (published-stream scatter per hand), plus scratchpad one-offs (gravity-parse, quat-fit) recorded in the transcript.

modo: T182: LAB, headset NOT connected -- Auto boot with no headset dead-ended the console, and the promised [s]+[Enter] skip did nothing either
driver: vr-boot-selector.sh Auto (default/timeout) -> power-on.py --pre-login, headset physically unplugged (0/5 lsusb), user at the physical machine, reported it live via chat
veredicto: REAL BUG, CAUGHT LIVE, ROOT-CAUSED WITH THE STUCK PROCESS STILL ON THE MACHINE. User report: picked/defaulted to Auto with the headset unplugged, the console 'quedo ahi' (just sat there) with no observed timeout, and [s]+[Enter] (the documented skip-to-2D key) did nothing. Checked the live tty1 session (still running from 09:32): power-on.py (pid 1172) was in ps state T (STOPPED), not sleeping/running -- the interpreter was not executing at all, which alone explains why neither its own 90s wait_for_reseat clock nor the outer `timeout 1200` ceiling ever fired. `ps -o pid,pgid,tpgid` showed the mechanism exactly: timeout (pid 1171) and python3 (1172) both sit in process group 1171, but the pty's foreground group (tpgid) is 1170 (the `sh -c` from `script -c` in vr-boot-selector.sh) -- a real, consequential split, not a no-op. ROOT CAUSE: GNU coreutils `timeout`, without --foreground, calls setpgid(0,0) on itself before running the monitored command, moving itself (and by inheritance its child) into a NEW process group that is never made the controlling terminal's foreground group. `/bin/sh` on this box is dash, and dash does NOT tail-exec-replace itself for a single-command `-c "..."` script the way bash sometimes does -- so `sh -c "timeout 1200 python3 ..."` really forks, and the split is real. The instant power-on.py's wait_for_reseat tries to read stdin -- ANY keystroke, plain Enter or the [s]+[Enter] skip alike -- the kernel's controlling-terminal rules fire SIGTTIN for a background-group read, whose default action is STOP. Not paused: stopped for good. A stopped process only acts on SIGCONT/SIGKILL; SIGTERM (what the outer `timeout 1200` sends on its own ceiling) just queues as pending and is never delivered while stopped -- so the '1200s hard ceiling, can't hang indefinitely' comment in the script was WRONG for this exact failure mode: the console can and did hang indefinitely, recoverable only by a human with root (getty@tty2, Ctrl+Alt+F2, `sudo kill -9 -1171`) or a reboot. REPRODUCED SYNTHETICALLY before touching anything live: a pty harness forking sh -c "timeout N python3 -c '<blocking read>'" reproduced the exact same pgid/tpgid split and the exact same ps state T the instant a line was written to the master side, 1:1 against the real stuck session's process tree; the same harness with `timeout --foreground` kept python3 in the terminal's foreground group and the read succeeded immediately. LIKELY explains T172's 'ya no pude apretar enter para volver a reintentar' too -- the WAIT_HUMAN_S rearm-on-Enter logic added that night never got a chance to run, because the very first Enter already froze the process before reaching it; T172 fixed the ceiling (120s -> 1200s) without ever finding this. FIX (patches/none needed, plain script change): added `--foreground` to both `timeout 1200` invocations in vr-boot-selector.sh (the `script`-wrapped one and the no-`script` fallback). Verified end-to-end in a pty harness running the REAL power-on.py with the fixed invocation, headset still unplugged: [1/5 census fails] -> reseat prompt shown -> wrote 's\n' -> 'SIN VR POR AHORA' printed immediately, process reached `systemctl isolate graphical.target` in state S+ (foreground, not T) instead of freezing. Also clarified wait_for_reseat's own prompt text (power-on.py): spells out 's, then Enter' instead of the bracket notation '[s]+[Enter]' the user flagged as an odd/ambiguous combo, and states the 90s unattended timeout up front instead of leaving it to be inferred from the countdown. NOT YET DONE: the vr-boot-selector.sh service's own installed unit (already `enabled`+`active` on this box) will pick up the fix on the NEXT boot automatically (ExecStart points straight at the repo path, no ~/vr/ copy involved for this script) -- not hot-reloaded into the CURRENTLY stuck session. That live session (pid 1172, stuck since 09:32) is still stuck as this entry is written and needs manual recovery (Ctrl+Alt+F2 -> login -> `sudo kill -9 -1171`, or a reboot) -- told to the user directly, not fixed remotely (no passwordless sudo from this agent's shell).

modo: T183: LAB -- validating the headset after T182 and today's Codex controller-calibration session; found a live USB2 companion HID storm instead, characterized it with real timing, and caught our own methodology error (constellation was off all night)
driver: lab-full monado e26ac16b3 (=0001-0047 + today's controller-calibration-telemetry-and-axis-ab-transforms patch), basalt 76d71a8 (=0001-0002), jack-in-wayland.sh 1 6dof, WMR_CONTROLLER_CALIBRATION_LOG=1 / WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1 / WMR_CONTROLLER_WMR_AXES=1 as noted per-launch, Propagation VR + SUPERHOT VR, scripts/hw-monitor.sh (new)
veredicto:
STARTED AS A SANITY CHECK, BECAME A REAL-TIME CABLE-VS-SOFTWARE DISCRIMINATION SESSION. First launch (constellation off, see methodology error below): panel showed backlight only despite DP lease/EDID/OpenXR session all reporting clean success -- the project's own core warning (CLAUDE.md, 'verification is physical') held exactly. Root cause: control_read_packets in wmr_hmd.c hit 152594 consecutive os_hid_read=-1 errors on the companion (03f0:0580) almost immediately after session start. User correctly pushed back and asked to rule out a missing-image software trap before accepting a hardware verdict -- verified clean (valid JPEG, loaded correctly, real swapchains, FOCUSED state, no throw) -- and the harder proof came from lsusb itself: the companion AND audio device fully vanished from the bus, not just failing HID reads. A mains power-cut (220V) fixed that instance's storm but a second backlight-only repeat showed ZERO companion errors -- genuinely two different failure signatures across two attempts, not the same bug recurring identically.

AT THE USER'S EXPLICIT REQUEST, kept testing IN the degraded state instead of reseating immediately, to determine whether this afternoon's WMR controller-calibration session (docs/33, done with Codex) might have captured contaminated data. Found a real, new class of silent corruption: with WMR_CONTROLLER_CALIBRATION_LOG=1, controller CALIB telemetry showed ori_tracked=1 while the raw IMU quaternion was bit-for-bit frozen for up to 196+ seconds straight, INCLUDING through 8s of the user actively waving both controllers -- proving it wasn't stillness, the fusion feed was genuinely stalled. Nothing in the reported pose flags this: ori_tracked=1 lies exactly like pos_tracked's already-documented placeholder pattern (docs/33) lies, just for a different field. Correlated live: launched Propagation VR and SUPERHOT (twice) during active storm, and the user's own in-game description ('left hand floating 5m away, always pointing forward', 'very smooth, no jumps') matched a frozen placeholder pose exactly -- the perceived smoothness WAS the freeze. Direct HID probe (preflight.sh, bypassing Monado) confirmed the controllers themselves stayed alive and responsive the whole time -- the freeze is internal to Monado's fusion thread, not a dead controller. Also measured monado-service at 237% CPU while otherwise idle (photo viewer only): control_read_packets has NO backoff on repeated companion read failures (confirmed reading the source) -- a real, separate software bug that likely amplifies how long a real dropout looks broken to the app layer, even though it doesn't create the underlying marginal contact. Not fixed tonight, flagged for later.

USER-DRIVEN HARDWARE INTERVENTIONS, mixed results, not monotonic: a first '220V + USB flip' made things WORSE at the topology level -- lsusb -t showed the USB3 SuperSpeed branch (bus004, 04b4:6504 + HoloLens Sensors) completely gone, with HoloLens Sensors falling back to 480M on the SAME USB2 hub as the companion -- a new, more severe failure mode never seen before in this project's cable saga. An identical second '220V + USB flip' recovered the correct topology (SuperSpeed branch back on bus004). So this specific intervention is NOT reliably idempotent -- it can make the connection worse before it makes it better. Neither reseated the visor-end connector itself; that's still untried tonight.

BUILT scripts/hw-monitor.sh (new, committed, synced to ~/vr/) to stop guessing at timing: a transition-only background logger (plus a coarse ~30s companion-error/imu_age_ms snapshot) so the log stays tiny (a few KB/hour) instead of raw-tailing jack-in-wayland.log, which itself hit 53.7 MB in ~19 minutes of active storm on a disk already at 91% (19GB free/207GB) -- compressed 55x to ~975KB with gzip, confirming it's cheap pure text to archive. With it running, got the project's first REAL timestamped answer to 'how long do the blips last': over 6+ minutes, the USB2 branch (companion+audio, hub 04b4:6506) blipped to 3/5 (once 2/5) for consistently ~3 seconds at a time, spaced 6-90s apart (commonly 25-60s); the USB3 branch (cameras/controller tunnel, docs/03) never moved once in the same window. But companion HID read-failures climbed at roughly 400-600/s nearly continuously, INCLUDING during 5/5-enumerated stretches between blips -- lsusb enumeration is NOT a reliable proxy for the companion channel's actual health, a real methodology correction for future sessions (use hw-monitor.sh's snapshot line instead).

SELF-CAUGHT METHODOLOGY ERROR, the most important correction of the night: jack-in-wayland.sh's 6dof mode defaults WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS to 0 unless explicitly overridden (line 283), and every launch until 23:24 omitted that flag -- meaning constellation-based controller POSITION tracking was never actually active. Every 'hands frozen at the placeholder position' observation reported to the user before that point (Propagation VR, two SUPERHOT sessions) was AT LEAST PARTLY just this default-off plain-3DoF behavior, not exclusively the USB storm -- a real overclaim already stated to the user as settled before being caught. vr-state.sh's own status line printed 'constellation=0' on every single check made that whole time; the pattern wasn't connected until the user's own live description ('solo sobre su eje') pointed straight at plain 3DoF. Corrected and re-tested: with WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1 set correctly, position jumps genuinely improved live in SUPERHOT (user: 'por lo general veo las manos donde corresponde, aun a veces saltan de lugar, pero notablemente menos') -- attributable to the gravity gate (patch 0047, WMR_CONSTELLATION_GRAVITY_GATE_DEG default 14deg, unconditionally active, confirmed reading the source, needed no new flag). Residual jumps match T181's already-documented open problem (near-pure-yaw mis-assignments, gravity-blind by construction).

Orientation was still wrong with constellation alone -- expected, since none of today's experimental axis-correction options (WMR_CONTROLLER_WMR_AXES, WMR_CONTROLLER_FULL_CAL_RIGHT/LEFT, all from the controller-calibration-telemetry-and-axis-ab-transforms patch, commit 36ff120) default to on -- all gated behind DEBUG_GET_ONCE_BOOL_OPTION(..., false). Tried WMR_CONTROLLER_WMR_AXES=1 live in SUPERHOT (T181's best-evidenced candidate, the Rx180 bridge, Wahba-fit at 178.9/178.8deg on both hands): did not clearly fix orientation, and the user's live read was that POSITION got WORSE with it applied. Not root-caused tonight -- the IMU-freeze pattern kept recurring in every configuration tried (with and without the axis fix, with and without constellation), muddying any clean before/after comparison. CONCLUSION, agreed live with the user: today's whole docs/33 controller-calibration session needs to be REDONE under stricter hygiene -- constellation explicitly on, samples gated on imu_age_ms freshness (not just pos_tracked/ori_tracked, which can both read true while stale/frozen), and ideally captured outside an active USB2 storm window (check hw-monitor.sh's live snapshot before trusting a capture). None of this afternoon's fitted transforms can be trusted as clean until redone this way.

PROCESS NOTE: the user's rule (Steam titles get closed by the user's own Force Quit in Steam, not by this agent running vr-state.sh --close-title) was violated twice tonight -- once corrected immediately by the user, once caught and flagged by the agent itself. vr-state.sh --close-title itself works cleanly every time it was used (begin/end session counts matched), so the rule is about who's driving, not that the script is unsafe.

OPEN FOR NEXT SESSION: the physical visor-end cable reseat was never actually attempted tonight (only PC-end power-cycle + USB-flip, with inconsistent, sometimes-worse results) -- still the next real step per docs/22's ladder, and given the user's own 'nunca me pasó que trackee tan mal', this may finally be the rev2A cable's moment rather than another reseat. control_read_packets's missing backoff (wmr_hmd.c) is a real, separate software bug worth fixing regardless of cable health. Redo the controller axis calibration (WMR_CONTROLLER_WMR_AXES and the FULL_CAL_* family) with imu_age_ms gating and constellation always explicitly on -- consider teaching wmr-fit-roll-axis.py and any future capture tooling to reject stale samples the same way docs/33 already says to reject placeholder positions. The USB2 blip's root physical cause (connector vs internal hub vs cable core) is still not localized, only characterized in time -- keep hw-monitor.sh running through the next physical reseat to see whether the blip pattern actually changes.

modo: T184: LAB -- USB-C orientation A/B protocol confirms a real, deterministic connector fault; port and visor-reseat rigorously cleared as unreliable fixes; rotation-speed hypothesis confirmed once storm noise dropped; a new unresolved height offset found
driver: lab-full monado e26ac16b3 (=0001-0047 + controller-calibration-telemetry-and-axis-ab-transforms), basalt 76d71a8, jack-in-wayland.sh 1 6dof, WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1, WMR_CONTROLLER_WMR_AXES=1 in two of the launches, SUPERHOT VR, scripts/hw-monitor.sh (transition-only monitor, now the primary live-diagnosis tool)
veredicto:
USER-DRIVEN, RIGOROUS: a tape-marked USB-C orientation A/B protocol (cold reinsert each trial, side recorded before checking the result) found a real, 100% reproducible connector fault on the USB-C plug from the headset's active-cable hub box into the PC: 'matched' side gave 0/5 (both branches fully dead) on EVERY cold reinsertion (6/6 across the night); 'unmatched' gave at least 2/5 (SuperSpeed branch -- 04b4:6504 + HoloLens Sensors 045e:0659 -- alive) on EVERY cold reinsertion, never less. This is not spec-compliant USB-C behavior (orientation should be electrically transparent) and is real, controlled evidence, not flapping noise.

TESTED AND RULED OUT AS RELIABLE FIXES, WITH DISCIPLINE: whether the USB2 branch (companion 03f0:0580 + audio 0bda:4c15, hub 04b4:6506) joins on top of the guaranteed SuperSpeed 2/5 -- giving the full 5/5 -- was tested against two candidate causes across four different PC USB ports and three separate visor-end reconnects, ALL while holding orientation fixed at 'unmatched'. Neither showed a clean causal effect: visor reseat was tried three times starting from a confirmed 2/5 state and never once produced a transition to 5/5 (2->2 every time); PC port changes showed the same non-effect in the one case tested cleanly from 2/5 (2->2), and the one case that looked like a fix (first port change, 3->5) was re-examined against exact before/after timestamps and the climb to 5/5 started BEFORE the port change was even completed -- coincidence with a spontaneous recovery, not causation. HONEST CONCLUSION, stated directly to the user rather than picking a lever to credit: getting from 2/5 to 5/5 has NO confirmed reliable trigger from tonight's data. It looks spontaneous, on a timescale of minutes, independent of which port or whether the visor was just reseated.

NEW WORKING HYPOTHESIS, the user's own idea, well-grounded rather than speculative: this cable is already documented (CLAUDE.md) as an ACTIVE cable with a DP-repeater box, and the USB hub chips seen in lsusb all night (Cypress CY4603 04b4:6506, HP WMR hub 04b4:6504) are real silicon with their own firmware/state machines -- not passive pins. A firmware/state-machine glitch in that hub silicon explains the pattern far better than mechanical wear: the user reports the cable has NEVER felt physically loose, has been pulled on hard with no effect, and ran rock-solid for hours at a time on Windows once a session was up -- inconsistent with ongoing mechanical marginal contact, but very consistent with an active component that occasionally needs a power-cycle-class event to clear a stuck state, and doesn't always clear even then. Reframes the fix target from 'replace/reseat the cable' to 'find what reliably resets the hub chip's firmware state' -- not identified tonight.

power-on.py's reseat_instructions() updated (this session, before this entry) with the orientation-flip step for the total-dead (0/5) case specifically, citing this A/B protocol -- the single-branch-missing cases already suggested the flip from the 2026-08-13 seat-lottery diagnosis (T171), now upgraded from a heuristic to a confirmed one. Deliberately did NOT add any 2/5->5/5 guidance -- honest per the finding above, nothing to recommend there yet.

SEPARATELY, once several extended clean (0-companion-error) windows opened up tonight thanks to the 'unmatched' orientation, TWO real tracking findings got their first uncontaminated look all project: (1) the user's rotation-speed hypothesis from earlier in the night ('gira lento, salta menos') held up live in SUPERHOT with real hardware noise mostly gone -- slow controller rotation tracks well, fast rotation makes it 'disparar para cualquier lado ... como si le faltara cuadros para dibujar en el medio' (feels like missing interpolation frames). This matches the already-documented ~4 solves/s per controller against 30Hz cameras (wmr_controller_base.c comment, 2026-08-12) and predicts near-pure-yaw mis-assignment (T181) landing more often when inter-frame rotation is larger, though this session did not capture new offline data to quantify it (the earlier rotexp capture, done inside the storm, stays inconclusive -- see the CALIB log's own placeholder/frozen-IMU samples dominating that window). (2) A genuinely NEW, previously-uninvestigated symptom: the user reported controller HEIGHT (vertical position) is also wrong, independent of the already-known lateral jump and rotation bugs -- 'nunca lo contemplamos bien'. A fork agent tasked with finding the likely code-level cause (camera extrinsics, XRT_TRACKING_ORIGIN_OFFSET_Y, constellation-vs-world frame mismatch) WENT OFF-TASK and returned a live storm status update instead of a code analysis -- a real, logged agent failure, not investigated further tonight. The height question is OPEN, unstarted.

WMR_CONTROLLER_WMR_AXES=1 (T181's Rx180 bridge) was tried live TWICE more tonight, once in a heavily-stormed window (contaminated, discounted) and once in a genuinely clean window (0 companion errors at launch). Both times the user's live verdict was that rotation was still wrong. Two independent looks, one clean, agreeing -- a real negative result, not just noise: this specific flag as currently implemented does not fix in-game controller orientation. docs/33's whole calibration session still needs the redo already planned in T183 (imu_age_ms gating, constellation always explicitly on) but this result should lower confidence in the Rx180 hypothesis itself, not just the data quality it was measured on.

ALSO CONFIRMED (fork agent, clean result this time): SUPERHOT VR ships no native recenter -- inspected all 11 of its binding files, only shoot/grab/mindwave/menu/ui_navigation exist. The only recenter live in this stack is the project's own patches/xrizer/0001 (hold-menu-3s), confirmed via the live xrizer log to have fired zero times this session -- rules out an accidental recenter as the explanation for any of tonight's observed jumps.

PROCESS/TOOLING: a genuine hygiene mistake this session -- scripts/hw-monitor.sh was promoted from a scratchpad one-off to a committed repo script mid-session, but the ALREADY-RUNNING scratchpad instance was never killed, so USB-transition data and ACTION markers were split across two separate log files (scratchpad vs ~/vr/logs/hw-monitor.log) for over an hour before being noticed and reconciled for the lever-discrimination analysis above. modo: T185: WINDOWS -- controlled USB-port-swap test rules out Windows device-identity (ContainerID/InstanceId) as the 422 mechanism; confirms it's the same USB2-branch enumeration fault as T184, now with port choice as a third trigger
driver: Oasis Driver unlock_wmr.exe (3 runs across the night) + PowerShell Get-PnpDevice / Get-PnpDeviceProperty -KeyName DEVPKEY_Device_ContainerId (no admin needed) on the lab's Windows-only nvme0n1p3 SSD, cross-checked against a live chntpw/reged export of the SYSTEM registry hive mounted read-only from the Linux side; G2 connected via its active-cable USB-C into two different rear, CPU/chipset-fed USB 3.x ports on the same PC
veredicto:
STARTED FROM THE USER'S OWN HYPOTHESIS ("esta aprovisionado aqui por tener cadena de hardwareids identica") AND DISPROVED IT CLEANLY, WHICH IS A GOOD RESULT: the 422 seen on a port change is NOT a Windows/Oasis identity-provisioning bug, it's the same physical enumeration fault this project has been chasing all week.

BASELINE (same port as the rest of the night, established first): unlock_wmr.exe reported "Headset is already unlocked!" and found BOTH controllers (healthiest state captured all session -- earlier runs only found Left). Get-PnpDevice/Get-PnpDeviceProperty across all 9 device nodes behind the active cable's hub (both the SuperSpeed/sensors branch, VID_045E&PID_0659, and the USB2/companion branch, VID_03F0&PID_0580) showed ONE shared ContainerID, {ee4482ce-afe7-5844-820a-73f26905a52f} -- confirmed (cross-checked against the registry export, see docs/31) to be the Cypress hub chip's own hardware serial, not anything port-derived. Top-level USB nodes use the device's own real serial as InstanceId directly (USB\VID_03F0&PID_0580\8CC044Z2CM, USB\VID_045E&PID_0659\BDA9EF65-...); only the HID-collection/interface child nodes use a hashed suffix (8&2513e90&0&0000 etc.), itself derived from the serial-based parent. Strong theoretical prediction going in: this whole identity chain should be port-independent.

TEST: SteamVR confirmed clean in the baseline port, closed, headset moved to a second, compatible, rear USB 3.x port on the same PC. SteamVR then threw error 422. A PowerShell capture taken in the new port was diffed PROGRAMMATICALLY (not eyeballed) against the baseline capture.

RESULT, exact: of 9 device-node lines, exactly 2 changed -- both belonging to the presence device (HID\VID_03F0&PID_0580\8&2513E90&0&0000 and USB\VID_03F0&PID_0580\8CC044Z2CM). Their InstanceId and ContainerId stayed BYTE-IDENTICAL to baseline; only their Status flipped from OK to Unknown. Nothing on the 045E/SuperSpeed branch moved at all. Status=Unknown on a device Get-PnpDevice can still enumerate by ID is the classic "ghost/non-present device" signature: Windows remembers the device's identity but it is not currently on the bus. I.e. the companion (03f0:0580) branch simply failed to enumerate in the new port -- not a rejected/mismatched identity, an absent one.

CONCLUSION: the ContainerID/instance-path hypothesis is dead as an explanation for port-triggered 422s -- identity survives a real port change intact, exactly as the registry mechanics predicted. What actually happened is the SAME USB2-branch-vs-SuperSpeed-branch split enumeration fault T184 already characterized (SuperSpeed rock solid, USB2/companion+audio unreliable) -- this test adds USB PORT CHOICE to the list of things that can trip it, alongside orientation. The underlying WHY (what makes one port/orientation reliably bring up the USB2 branch and another not) is still unexplained -- this test narrows the suspect list, it doesn't close the case. User did not bother re-testing SteamVR after seeing the Unknown status ("ya ni probe steam, sabemos que ocurre") -- correct call, the PowerShell data alone already explains the 422 fully.

METHODOLOGY NOTE, worth keeping: the first attempted post-swap PowerShell capture the user pasted was byte-for-byte identical to the baseline (diffed and confirmed identical) -- the user's own instinct ("revisa si no es identica, capaz copie mal") caught what turned out to be a copy-paste accident, not a real second measurement, BEFORE it got treated as a null result. Second, careful capture is what's recorded above. Also worth keeping for any future registry work: raw strings/byte-proximity search on a live registry hive is unreliable (value names are narrow/8-bit not UTF-16, and a value's cell isn't reliably near its key name) -- `chntpw`'s `reged -x` gives a clean structured export instead, that's how the baseline ContainerID/InstanceId ground truth was actually established before this test ever ran.

OPEN: reconnecting to the original port to confirm symmetric recovery (would close the loop the way T184's A/B protocol did) was not yet done this session -- natural next step whenever picked back up. Full verbatim device paths, the HololensSensors.inf/HmdMonitors.inf cross-reference, and the registry export methodology are in docs/31's "Live capture, 2026-08-16" section.

CLOSED OUT, same session: reconnected to the ORIGINAL port. Checked from the Linux side this time (different OS, different tool -- udev/sysfs via lsusb, not PowerShell/PnP -- genuine cross-validation, not a repeat of the same measurement): full 5/5 clean (companion 03f0:0580, audio 0bda:4c15, both hub personas 04b4:6506/6504, sensors 045e:0659), sysfs mtimes ~3.5 min old at check time, matching the user's own reconnect timing. The ghosted branch came back clean on its own once back in the original port -- symmetric recovery confirmed, no unlock_wmr.exe re-run needed this time to get Linux-side enumeration back (Windows-side Oasis behavior after reconnect not re-tested, not needed to close this specific loop).

SCOPE CHECK, worth stating plainly so this doesn't get overclaimed later: this test did NOT solve the project's actual open problem, which is still exactly where it was before tonight -- WHY the USB2/companion branch sometimes fails to enumerate and sometimes doesn't, and how to reliably force it to join. What got resolved tonight is narrower: a competing hypothesis that emerged FROM tonight's own photos ("maybe it's a missing software provisioning/registration step, not hardware") was tested and killed. `unlock_wmr.exe` succeeding is downstream of the companion device actually being enumerated, not a separate cause of it -- the tool confirms hardware state, it doesn't fix it. Net effect: the original hardware hypothesis (active-cable hub firmware/state-machine glitch) survives, gains a second confirmed trigger (USB port choice, alongside T184's orientation), and still has zero confirmed fix. Don't read this entry as "the cable issue is understood" -- it's "one wrong turn is now ruled out, the real question is exactly as open as it was at T184."

modo: T186: LAB (Linux) -- PC-end USB-C disconnect/reconnect, same port, same orientation, is 6/6 reliable at bringing up the full 5/5 branch, in sharp contrast to T184's 0/3 for visor-end reseat
driver: lab-full, headset already at a known-good 5/5 baseline (same port/orientation as the rest of tonight, T184/T185), G2 idle (no monado-service running), cold PC-end unplug (~8-10s fully disconnected) + reconnect in the SAME port and SAME orientation each time, checked live via `lsusb` immediately after each reconnect (device numbers bumping each trial confirms genuine fresh re-enumeration, not stale/cached output)
veredicto:
USER'S OWN LIVE OBSERVATION ("pulling the cable Jack-Sparrow-style and nothing happens") PROMPTED THIS TEST, AND IT LANDED CLEAN: 6/6 trials, every single one 5/5 immediately (all of companion 03f0:0580, audio 0bda:4c15, both hub personas 04b4:6506/6504, sensors 045e:0659 present at first lsusb check post-reconnect, no settle-time needed). Device/bus numbers strictly incrementing across trials (013-015/006-007 through 028-030/016-017) -- proof each reconnect was a genuine fresh USB enumeration event, not a leftover kernel cache reporting the same devices as still present.

WHY THIS MATTERS, set against everything already on record tonight and in T184: T184 rigorously tested VISOR-END reseat as a 2/5->5/5 trigger, holding orientation fixed at 'unmatched' -- 0/3, never worked. This test isolates the OTHER end of the same cable -- PC-end USB-C unplug/replug, same port, same orientation -- and gets the opposite result, 6/6. The two ends of the cable behave completely differently as levers, which had never been directly contrasted with matched rigor before tonight. Consistent with (not a new finding on its own, but now measured with real numbers behind it) the standing hypothesis that this is active silicon (the Cypress hub in the inline box) with a state-machine/enumeration quirk, not a marginal mechanical contact -- docs/22's old observation that the user has pulled hard on the cable with zero effect, and tonight's own live version of the same thing, both point at a connection-establishment-time fault, not an ongoing-contact one.

SCOPE, stated precisely so it doesn't get overclaimed: this is 6/6 reliability for PC-end reconnect specifically AT a port/orientation combination already known good going in (the one T184/T185 used all night). It does NOT show PC-end reconnect can rescue a bad orientation ('matched', per T184) or a bad port (per T185's ghosted companion) -- that's a distinct, untested question. What IS now a strong, well-evidenced, low-cost recommendation: when the USB2 branch is missing (2/5 or similar), the first thing to try is a full PC-end USB-C unplug + ~10s wait + replug in the SAME port/orientation, before reaching for a port change, an orientation flip, or a visor-end reseat -- cheapest lever, and the only one so far measured at 100% in its tested condition. Worth folding into `power-on.py`'s guidance for the 2/5 case specifically (currently only guides on 0/5 dead-panel, per last session's header) if this holds up under a wider test (different starting orientation/port).

modo: T187: WINDOWS -- real gameplay session on top of the T186-validated 5/5 state runs clean, no drops; first night this project has both a repeatable trigger AND a real-load confirmation together
driver: Windows side, same physical box, headset left connected after T186's 6/6 PC-end-reconnect test (already at a known-good, fingerprinted state -- see docs/22's new 'Known-good fingerprint' section), user launched and played a real SteamVR/Oasis title through a full session rather than just checking menus
