modo: T188: LAB (Linux) -- caught the T183 companion-storm/CPU-spin bug live and full-scale for the first time under real gameplay, with three independent physical confirmations (audio, head drift, cooler noise); shut down manually, never self-resolved
driver: lab-full, jack-in-wayland.sh 1 6dof via vr-launcher.py (Aircar, appid 1073390), first plain launch then a relaunch with WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1 + WMR_CONTROLLER_CALIBRATION_LOG=1, scripts/hw-monitor.sh running throughout (bug-fixed same session, see the usb3_branch regex note below) as the sole instrument -- this is the first time this project caught the T183 storm from cold start to shutdown with continuous timestamped data plus live user-reported physical symptoms, not a postmortem log read
veredicto:
TIMELINE: first Aircar session (no constellation) ran clean at first, but hw-monitor's own snapshot line caught companion_errors silently climbing (0 -> 18688 -> 27604 -> 36525) WHILE lsusb kept reading 5/5 the whole time -- two brief self-recovering 3/5 dips (~3s each) during this window, easy to miss without the snapshot line, exactly the blind spot this project already flagged ('5/5 is not proof the companion channel is healthy'). User closed that session via Steam Force Quit; monado-service (separate process) kept running with the storm already in progress. Relaunch with constellation+calibration-log on triggered the expected transient 3/5 dip from the kill/restart panel-power-cycle (recovered 3s, normal, already documented), companion_errors reset to 0 with the fresh process -- but the storm restarted almost immediately (8183 errors by 23s in) and never stopped for the rest of the 17-minute session.

MEASURED, full scale for the first time: companion_errors climbed continuously to a peak of 472175 before manual shutdown -- MORE THAN 3x T183's 152594, which is the number that led to a full backlight-only panel lockup that same prior session. monado-service CPU held between 411-432% throughout (one thread pinned 99%+), matching and exceeding T183's 237% figure. A genuine controller IMU freeze hit both hands simultaneously, imu_age_ms climbing from fresh (25-40ms) to 235918ms (~4 minutes stale) between 04:22:48 and 04:26:23, then self-recovering (left first, then right) and staying fresh for the remaining ~4 minutes -- a transient freeze episode nested inside the larger, non-transient CPU/error storm, distinct symptoms on their own clocks. USB branch drops (USB CHANGE transitions) numbered 70 total (~35 drop/recover cycles) across the ~19-minute window from first symptom to shutdown, NOT evenly spaced -- clustered denser and reached lower minimums (down to 2/5 multiple times) as the session went on: roughly one cycle per 40s early, six cycles in the final 90 seconds before shutdown. The trend was monotonically worsening the entire time it was observed, at no point stabilizing or improving on its own.

THREE INDEPENDENT PHYSICAL CONFIRMATIONS, live, from the user, each volunteered before being asked about that specific symptom: (1) audio output silently jumped from the headset's own speakers to the PC's desktop speakers mid-session, user confirmed touching nothing -- matches the already-documented PipeWire-sink-recreation mechanism (T052-T057) triggered by the USB2/audio device (0bda:4c15, same branch as the companion) being disturbed. (2) Head position drift got noticeably worse ('se va hacia arriba con vueltas') starting at approximately the same moment as the audio jump -- SLAM/Basalt runs on a SEPARATE USB branch (SuperSpeed/045e:0659) from the companion storm, so this is not a direct USB-contention explanation; the standing hypothesis is CPU contention, since Basalt's queue-latency sensitivity was already established in T180 and a thread pinned at 99% competing for the same cores is a plausible, not yet proven, bridge between the two branches' symptoms. (3) The CPU cooler's fan was heard ramping up progressively louder during the incident and quieting down immediately after monado-service was stopped -- independent, non-digital confirmation that the measured CPU percentages were real physical load, not a monitoring artifact.

NEVER SELF-RESOLVED: closing Aircar (both via vr-state.sh --close-title and, redundantly, the user's own Steam Force Quit) had ZERO effect on the storm -- companion_errors kept climbing at the same rate straight through both closes, confirming the spin lives inside monado-service's own control_read_packets loop (T183's diagnosis), entirely independent of whether any OpenXR client is connected. Only a clean SIGTERM to monado-service itself stopped it. This closes an open question from T183's own writeup: the no-backoff CPU spin bug there was found but 'not fixed yet, a real target for next session regardless of cable health' -- it still is not fixed, but tonight is the first time its real-world severity ceiling was measured (padding past the previous worst case) and its complete independence from the client/game layer was directly confirmed rather than inferred.

TOOLING NOTE: hw-monitor.sh's usb3_branch sub-metric had a live regex bug fixed mid-session (2-digit device-number assumption broken by tonight's earlier 6-reconnect test pushing device numbers past 9) -- caught and fixed BEFORE this incident's data was collected, so the companion_errors/imu_age_ms/main usb=X/5 figures in this entry are all trustworthy; only usb3_branch briefly showed a false 0/2 in the pre-fix window, already noted and corrected in real time.

OPEN, unchanged from T183: control_read_packets still has no backoff on repeated companion read failures -- this needs a real code fix, not another workaround. Whether constellation being ON specifically triggers or worsens this storm is NOT established -- the storm was already climbing during the FIRST session, before constellation was ever enabled, so constellation's role (if any) is contributory/coincidental until tested in isolation (constellation on/off, otherwise identical conditions, not done tonight).

modo: T189: LAB (Linux, 'dev' setup) -- isolated idle test confirms the companion storm needs NO tracking load, NO app, NO user interaction to happen; also splits the storm itself from the CPU-spin bug, which does NOT reproduce here
driver: jack-in-wayland.sh 1 3dof with WMR_SLAM=0 WMR_CAMERAS=0 (no SLAM, no constellation, no app launched), monado-service left running completely idle, hw-monitor.sh as the sole instrument, user explicitly not touching headset/controllers for the duration
veredicto:
DIRECT ANSWER TO THE QUESTION T188 LEFT OPEN AND docs/22's parked-test list named: the companion storm reproduces in the most minimal condition tested all project -- bare 3dof, no cameras, no SLAM thread, no constellation, no OpenXR client connected at all, headset physically untouched. companion_errors climbed from 0 (04:58:07) to 96927 (05:03:12), roughly 370-450/s, statistically indistinguishable from T188's rate under full load. USB branch drops (3/5, 2/5) recurred throughout on the same cadence as before. This settles it: the storm is NOT a function of tracking load, constellation, or application activity -- it happens exactly as readily at complete rest. Consistent with (does not newly prove, but removes a competing explanation for) the standing active-cable-hub-firmware hypothesis, and directly explains why T052-T057 (weeks ago) already caught this same signature at total idle with nothing running -- that was never an anomaly needing its own explanation, it's the SAME bug, always available to trigger, load or no load.

NEW SPLIT, not previously separated: monado-service's CPU stayed at 0.9-1.2% for the entire idle test -- NOT the 400%+ pin seen in T188 under Aircar+constellation. Companion_errors climbed at a comparable rate in both cases, so the storm itself and the CPU spin are not the same fixed pair they looked like in T188's writeup. Working read: the underlying companion-read-failure condition (control_read_packets hitting errors, T183's original find) is the constant, load-independent phenomenon: this session shows it climbing the counter without much CPU cost. Whatever pins CPU to 400%+ under an active session is a SEPARATE, still-uncharacterized mechanism layered on top -- possibly a different, more aggressive retry path taken only when something (SLAM, constellation, or the app itself) is also actively polling/reading from Monado concurrently with the failing companion reads, creating contention rather than a pure spin. Not root-caused; the isolating condition (idle, no load) that would let someone read the actual code path with a profiler while it's cheap to run is exactly the state captured in this entry.

OPEN, sharpened by this result: what CPU-load condition, if any, is required to turn the load-independent companion-error counter into the load-dependent 400%+ CPU pin -- test constellation-only (SLAM off) and SLAM-only (constellation off) in isolation, each at idle with no app, to bracket it further.

modo: T190: LAB ('dev' setup) -- completed the isolation matrix for the companion storm vs CPU cost; the storm is universal (all 3 isolated conditions), the 400%+ CPU pin needs the full combination, not any single piece
driver: Three back-to-back idle sessions, same headset/port/orientation throughout, hw-monitor.sh as the sole instrument, no app launched in any of them, user not touching headset/controllers: (a) plain 3dof (WMR_SLAM=0 WMR_CAMERAS=0), (b) SLAM-only/6dof head (WMR_CAMERAS on, Basalt running, WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS defaults off), (c) constellation-only ('ctrl' tracking mode -- cameras streaming, Basalt NOT loaded, WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1 by that mode's own default). Each run 1-2 minutes, immediately following the previous with a clean SIGTERM+relaunch.
veredicto:
FULL COMPARISON TABLE (monado-service %CPU, companion_errors climb rate):
  3dof only            ~1%      ~370-450/s
  SLAM only (6dof head) ~227-230% (flat, not escalating over 2+ min) ~200-250/s
  constellation only    ~20.7%   ~237/s
  SLAM+constellation+Aircar (T188) 400-432%, ESCALATING over 17 min  ~260-650/s, escalating

TWO CONCLUSIONS, cleanly separated for the first time: (1) the companion storm itself is
universal -- present at a broadly similar rate (200-450/s) in EVERY condition tested,
including total idle with zero tracking subsystems running. It does not need SLAM,
constellation, or an app to happen; T052-T057 already showed this weeks ago at total system
idle, and this matrix confirms it holds even with Monado itself up but doing nothing. (2) The
400%+ CPU pin from T188 is NOT explained by any single subsystem in isolation -- SLAM alone
caps around 227% (matches T163's already-documented ~1 core for Basalt), constellation alone
is much cheaper at ~21%, and neither shows any sign of climbing toward 400%+ even given 1-2
minutes to develop, unlike T188 where the figure kept climbing for the full 17-minute session.
Simple addition of the two isolated baselines (227+21=248) still falls well short of T188's
peak. The extreme CPU cost specifically needs the FULL combination (SLAM + constellation +
a real running application) -- not proven why, but the two-variable isolation is now
exhausted; whatever's left is either a genuine three-way interaction (contention between
Basalt's thread, the constellation solver, and the game's own CPU draw) or something tied to
session duration/escalation that a 1-2 minute isolated window is too short to reproduce even
under the right subsystem combination.

PRACTICAL UPSHOT for this project's own risk assessment: a bare head-tracking-only (SLAM,
no constellation) session is measurably safer on the CPU-spin front than a full
SLAM+constellation+game session, even though BOTH will show the companion storm climbing in
the background either way. If constellation isn't needed for a given title (most of docs/23's
catalog doesn't use hand-tracked visuals), leaving it off is a real, cheap mitigation against
the worst-case CPU pin, even though it does nothing for the underlying storm itself.

OPEN: whether a LONGER SLAM-only or constellation-only session (matching T188's 17-minute
duration, not just 1-2 minutes) eventually also climbs toward 400%+, or whether the
combination is genuinely required regardless of duration -- not tested, the isolated runs
tonight were short by comparison and this is the most direct remaining gap.

modo: T191: everyday system (community/comms session, lab disk mounted rw at /mnt/lab) -- wrote and compile-checked the T183/T188 companion-device backoff fix, no hardware run involved
driver: control_read_packets() in wmr_hmd.c, edited directly on the mounted lab disk's ~/vr/monado (lab-full) and fast-forwarded into the everyday system's own ~/Documents/linux_vr_base/monado clone (same branch); syntax/type-checked by invoking the exact compiler command from the lab build's compile_commands.json against the mounted paths, not a real ninja build and not run against hardware from this session
veredicto:
T188/T183's standing open item -- control_read_packets() swallows every companion-device os_hid_read failure forever with no counter, no cap, no pacing, on the (now-disproven) assumption that the shared thread loop stays paced by the hololens sensors device's blocking 100ms read. Added companion_consecutive_read_errors (mirrors hololens_consecutive_read_errors from 0036/e39af9683), escalates the log from silent WMR_DEBUG to WMR_WARN on the 1st and every 1000th consecutive failure, and once the count passes 50 sleeps 10ms on the failure path -- but, unlike 0036, NEVER gives up or kills the thread, since the companion device (IPD/proximity/screen-enable only) isn't load-bearing for tracking. Compiled clean with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic (the project's own build flags), zero warnings. Exported as patches/monado/0049. Committed as 657bcd8af on lab-full in both monado checkouts (lab disk and everyday system).

NOT DONE: no real-hardware run. This session's Bash tool is on the everyday system's KDE/X11 install and can only read/write the lab disk's files as a mounted filesystem -- it cannot boot or run the lab OS's own monado-service against real hardware to reproduce T188's load pattern (SLAM + constellation + a real app) and confirm the CPU pin is actually gone. That verification is the concrete next step for whoever is next on the lab machine itself.

Also drafted (not yet posted -- gitlab.freedesktop.org's web UI was returning 504s when this was written) a reply for MR !2967 citing T188's numbers and this fix, to answer Jan Schmidt's outstanding request there for evidence the companion-device transient-error path actually recovers. See project_g2_controller_6dof.md (assistant memory) for the draft text if it's needed again.

modo: T192: LAB (Linux) -- hardware verification of the 0049 companion-device backoff fix (T191), reproducing T188's exact load (SLAM + constellation + real app, single continuous session); fix confirmed working for its intended purpose, but the session surfaced a separate, more serious, previously-uncharacterized SLAM pose-rate collapse that is NOT caused by 0049 and remains unresolved
driver: Rebuilt ~/vr/monado first (T191's compile-check was never a real ninja build -- the on-disk monado-service binary predated the 0049 commit by ~30h; caught before launching anything). Single clean jack-in-wayland.sh 1 6dof launch (mode 1/90Hz, WMR_SLAM=1, SLAM_THREADS=2, basalt-g2-config.json) with WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1 set from the start (no mid-session relaunch, unlike T188's two-phase launch), immediately followed by Aircar (appid 1073390) via steam -applaunch. hw-monitor.sh and a custom companion_errors/CPU Monitor tallying monado-service's own %CPU and grepping jack-in-wayland.log directly. SLAM_WRITE_CSVS=1 (default on) recorded full pose/timing CSVs to logs/slam-20260816-184002/.
veredicto:
PRIMARY RESULT -- 0049 VERIFIED WORKING AS DESIGNED: monado-service ran continuously for the FULL session (39+ min, more than 2x T188's ~17min) without ever needing a SIGTERM. companion_consecutive_read_errors backoff confirmed actually engaging live: WMR_WARN escalation lines appear at exactly 1, 1000, 2000, 3000... consecutive failures as coded, and once past the 50-failure threshold the companion-error log-line rate self-capped at a measured, live-sampled ~100-105 lines/s (three 1s samples: 105, 104, 215) -- matching the 10ms os_nanosleep backoff's theoretical ~100Hz ceiling almost exactly. companion_errors climbed steadily throughout (the storm itself is universal/expected per T189/T190, 0049 was never meant to stop it) but monado-service CPU NEVER escalated -- it peaked around 551% in the first ~90s (SLAM+constellation alone, before Aircar fully loaded) and then trended steadily DOWNWARD for the rest of the session: 551%->510%->476%->456%->438%->423%->414%->407%->403%->402%->400%->393%->392% at the 39min mark. This is the opposite of T188's pattern (continuous climb to 472175 errors / 400-432% CPU pinned, needing SIGTERM). USB2 branch (bus 3: companion+audio+hub 04b4:6506) kept cycling at the same universal rate as T183/T188/T189/T190 (reconstructed via journalctl -k for a gap window, see METHODOLOGY NOTE below: ~55-58 disconnect/reconnect cycles in 24min, ~1 cycle/25s, matching history); USB3 branch (bus 4, SLAM/controller tunnel) had zero transitions, also matching history. Conclusion: 0049 does exactly what it was written to do -- prevents the unbounded CPU spin -- without introducing an obvious new failure of its own in this run.

METHODOLOGY NOTE (self-caught mistake): hw-monitor.sh's own background instance failed to actually start for the first ~24 minutes of the session -- two nohup attempts used the non-flat path (~/vr/scripts/hw-monitor.sh), which doesn't exist in the lab's flat ~/vr/ deployment (only ~/vr/hw-monitor.sh does), so both silently errored 'No such file or directory' while unrelated --mark calls using the correct flat path kept succeeding and masked the gap. Caught by noticing the log's last real line was a stale timestamp from hours earlier. Fixed mid-session (correct path, confirmed running); the missed window's USB transitions were reconstructed independently via `journalctl -k`, so no real data was lost, but this is the same class of 'confirm the monitor actually started' mistake the project has hit before (T183's own footnote about a split log from an unnoticed duplicate instance) -- opposite failure mode this time (silently NEVER started, vs. silently duplicated), same root lesson.

METHODOLOGY GAP FLAGGED BY THE USER, not yet closed: T192 vs T188 is a cross-session comparison (different boot, different day-part, different launch sequence -- T188 was a two-phase launch with a mid-session kill+relaunch; T192 was a single continuous launch), not a controlled same-day A/B. The user's own pushback, and correct: absence of runaway here doesn't by itself prove 0049 is the reason, only that this particular run didn't runaway. Response: built the pre-0049 parent commit (e26ac16b3, i.e. HEAD~1 from 657bcd8af) in an isolated git worktree (`git worktree add /tmp/monado-pre0049 657bcd8af^`), configured with the same `default` CMake preset, built with `ninja -j2` (deliberately throttled to avoid perturbing the live CPU measurement) to `/tmp/monado-pre0049/build/src/xrt/targets/service/monado-service`. NOT yet run. This is the named next step to actually close the A/B: swap this binary in via jack-in-wayland.sh's SERVICE path (or a temporary copy over the built one) and repeat the EXACT same single-clean-launch sequence used here.

SECONDARY, UNPLANNED FINDING -- SLAM POSE-RATE COLLAPSE, separate from 0049, NOT YET EXPLAINED: partway through the session the user reported real head-tracking lag ('mucho delay... como si se moviera bien, pero luego de 1 segundo cuando movi la cabeza'). Measured precisely from tracking.csv (SLAM_WRITE_CSVS output): pose interval was healthy and stable at ~55-58ms (~17-18Hz, matches the T180/T162-documented baseline) for the first 6m55s of the session, then abruptly and permanently collapsed at 18:46:56 (computed from CLOCK_MONOTONIC timestamps against `uptime -s`) to a suspiciously tight, near-constant ~632-648ms interval (~1.5-1.6Hz, jitter roughly +-1%) that persisted for the ENTIRE remainder of the ~39+ minute session -- including through the user explicitly stopping gameplay and several more minutes of the headset sitting completely untouched. Zero self-recovery observed at any point up to the last check. CORRECTION mid-session: an earlier verbal narrative in this same conversation wrongly attributed the collapse's ONSET to the moment the user began a deliberate 'real flight' stress test (~22-23min mark) -- that was an eyeballed guess from a coarse sample-count-bucketed CSV summary, which is a misleading proxy for wall-clock time once the tail of the file is dominated by 10x-longer-duration samples. The precise timestamp math places the actual onset at 6m55s in, i.e. well before the deliberate stress test and likely coincident with ordinary early Aircar gameplay -- a materially different, more concerning finding (bug is not exotic-stress-only, it showed up almost immediately and never let go).

INVESTIGATED AND RULED OUT as the direct cause: 0049's own control_read_packets() code. control_read_packets() and hololens_sensors_read_packets() (the function that actually carries IMU/camera-tunnel data) run strictly sequentially in ONE thread (wmr_run_thread, confirmed by reading the loop) and share wh->hid_lock, so the hypothesis was that 0049's unconditional 10ms os_nanosleep on every failing companion read (which fires continuously once the -- universal, expected -- storm passes 50 consecutive failures, i.e. almost immediately) could be starving the shared loop and indirectly throttling IMU delivery to Basalt. Live-measured against this: the companion-error log-line rate (a direct proxy for wmr_run_thread's own loop rate) is a healthy, steady ~100-105Hz throughout, matching the sleep's own theoretical cap with NO macro-scale stalling -- ruling out the read loop itself as the site of the 632ms stall. The bottleneck is downstream, most likely in Basalt's own SLAM processing or CPU-scheduling contention under the full SLAM+constellation+app combination -- a mechanism T188 ALREADY flagged as live but unproven ('head position drift... CPU contention... plausible, not proven'), now measured with hard numbers for the first time but still not root-caused.

ALSO USER-REPORTED, separate and not yet characterized: a distinct, previously-unremarked symptom -- a marked positional 'tick' in head pose with a period a bit under 1 second ('un paso un poco mas corto que 1 segundo'), reported as persisting regardless of headset orientation/movement, and explicitly noted by the user as recurring across multiple past sessions, not unique to tonight. Logged but not investigated numerically this session.

OPEN, in priority order for next session: (1) run the pre-0049 binary already built at /tmp/monado-pre0049 through the identical single-clean-launch sequence to determine whether the SLAM pose-rate collapse ALSO happens without 0049 -- given the read-loop-rate evidence above, this is expected to reproduce (implying it's a pre-existing, independent bug), but is not yet confirmed; (2) if confirmed pre-existing, profile/trace Basalt's own pipeline (timing.csv is already being recorded alongside tracking.csv) to find which stage actually backs up at the 6m55s mark; (3) characterize the separate sub-1s positional tick with the same CSV-based method that worked here; (4) the Jan Schmidt MR !2967 reply is STILL PENDING -- 0049's own verification is now clean, but this session's new finding means the reply, when posted, should not imply the headset's tracking is fully healthy, only that the specific companion-read CPU-spin 0049 targets is fixed.

modo: T193: LAB (Linux) -- the pre-0049 A/B the user asked for in T192, closing the loop on both open questions. Three attempts before a valid comparison; the valid one (45m47s, longer than the 0049 arm and including real gameplay) never reproduced EITHER of T188's symptoms, which complicates rather than confirms the original story
driver: Backed up the 0049 monado-service binary, swapped in the pre-0049 build (commit e26ac16b3 = 657bcd8af^, built earlier in /tmp/monado-pre0049 via git worktree) into ~/vr/monado/build in place, then ran the exact same launch recipe as T192's own 0049 arm (jack-in-wayland.sh 1 6dof, WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1, Aircar via steam -applaunch) repeatedly across three attempts as confounds were found and removed.
veredicto:
ATTEMPT 1 -- INVALIDATED, a real methodology catch: launched with the swapped binary and got a clean run (CPU ~250%, SLAM CSV healthy 12000+ samples, no collapse) -- but grep of the log showed left/right controller registration as None the WHOLE time. Constellation had zero devices to track (0 pushPose/blob-match lines in the entire log), so this wasn't the SLAM+constellation+app combo at all, just SLAM+app -- explains both the low CPU (half the 0049 arm's opening ~550%) and the lack of collapse. Caught before drawing any conclusion from it. Lesson: verify controller registration in the log before trusting ANY future run of this kind.

ATTEMPT 2 -- user powered both controllers back on, restarted: clean, both registered ('HP Reverb G2 Left/Right Controller'), CPU opened at 421-425% (much closer to the 0049 arm's 510-551% opening, same order of magnitude). Ran ~12 minutes healthy (SLAM CSV, no collapse) before the user reported 'los joy se apagaron' -- both VR controllers auto-standbying, consistent with the documented ~15min-idle timeout counted from physical power-on (which happened before the relaunch, not at Aircar's launch). User also proposed removing Aircar's own Xbox 360 gamepad (045e:028e, required for the game's own input per docs/23) as an additional controlled variable, suspecting it specifically. Session ended here to restart clean.

Getting to attempt 3 took ~6 wasted restart cycles fighting an unusually DENSE USB2-storm window (independent of either binary) -- companion device flapping 2/5-4/5 repeatedly, controllers failing to register at all in several attempts, one attempt independently hitting the already-documented 'left wins the controller startup race' bug on top of the storm. Battery swap on one controller (user's own diagnosis) didn't clear it. A single 220V mains power-cycle on the headset did, immediately -- USB back to stable 5/5, both controllers registered clean on the very next attempt. Reconfirms the project's own standing lesson (T052 era): don't hammer monado-service restarts against an actively dense storm window, it doesn't help.

ATTEMPT 3 -- THE VALID RUN: pre-0049 binary, both controllers registered clean, no Xbox 360 gamepad connected, Aircar launched and actually played for real (user confirmed active driving from roughly the 30-32min mark through the end). Total session length 45m47s -- LONGER than the original 0049 T192 arm's ~39min, and including a real-play phase the 0049 arm's own collapse had already PRECEDED (not followed). Final numbers: CPU opened ~357%, sat essentially flat 417-431% through the idle/out-of-focus first ~28 minutes (matching the shape, if not the exact level, of the 0049 arm's own idle stretch), then climbed gently to 481% once real driving started, and stayed there -- never approached runaway, no SIGTERM needed, ended by choice not by failure. companion_errors reached 893706 by the end -- nearly double T188's own peak of 472175, ~4x the 0049 arm's final count at a comparable point in real time -- with, again, no CPU consequence beyond the same mild climb. **THE DECISIVE RESULT: the SLAM pose-rate collapse (tracking.csv gap analysis) did NOT reproduce ANYWHERE in this session -- 37848 samples across the full 45m47s, zero gaps exceeding 300ms.** The 0049 arm's collapse hit hard and permanently at 6m55s and never recovered for the rest of its session; this longer, harder-loaded, higher-error-count run on the OTHER binary never showed it once.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR T192's TWO OPEN QUESTIONS: (1) SLAM collapse -- this directly CONTRADICTS the 'shared 100Hz-capped read loop, pure CPU contention, independent of which binary' explanation floated in T192 (which was based on measuring the loop's own rate, not on an A/B). The empirical result now points the other way: something links the collapse to 0049 specifically, or to some OTHER difference in that one original session, not to a universal SLAM-under-load phenomenon -- because a longer, harder-loaded run on the code WITHOUT 0049 simply didn't have it. This makes the mechanism MORE puzzling, not less, since the direct code read still shows no obvious way 0049's isolated 10ms sleep in control_read_packets could reach into Basalt's own pipeline. (2) CPU runaway -- STILL fully open. T188's own signature (continuous escalation to 400-432%, needing SIGTERM) has now failed to reproduce in THREE separate single-clean-launch sessions tonight, on both binaries. This is real evidence that T188's runaway depended on something specific to that night's own two-phase kill+relaunch launch pattern, not on the mere absence of backoff -- the A/B as run tonight (single clean launches both times) cannot actually distinguish '0049 fixed it' from 'it never happens under a single clean launch regardless of the code'.

ALSO RECONFIRMED, unrelated to 0049 -- patch 0023's known divergence-then-silent-reset: the user felt the in-game view suddenly 'fly off' mid-session and wasn't sure if it was a game feature. Checked directly against tracking.csv's raw position column (not just interval): SLAM position climbed from 0.24m to 31.26m over ~120 samples (a real divergence event), then snapped instantly back to 0.024m -- textbook 'implied speed > 10 m/s' auto-reset (patch 0023) firing exactly as designed, just as silently as T162 already documented ('a reset re-anchors at the origin without telling the application, so the world anchor teleports'). Not a new bug, not related to 0049, still not fixed (the real fix -- carrying the reset offset through to the output pose -- was never implemented).

OPEN, next steps in priority order: (1) repeat the 0049 arm FRESH under today's now-proven-clean conditions (both controllers registered, no gamepad, quiet storm window) -- if the SLAM collapse reproduces reliably a second time under 0049, that's much stronger evidence it's really linked to the fix (via a mechanism still to be found); if it doesn't, T192's original collapse may itself have been a one-off artifact of that session's own particular conditions. (2) To settle the CPU-runaway question properly, deliberately reproduce T188's exact two-phase launch pattern (start without constellation, let it run, kill, relaunch WITH constellation) on both binaries -- a single clean launch, tried three times tonight across two binaries, has not been the right experiment to isolate 0049's effect on that specific failure mode. (3) patch 0023's divergence-reset-without-anchor-carry-through is still open and was reconfirmed live tonight.

modo: T194: LAB (Linux) -- minimal isolation of T192/T193's SLAM pose-rate collapse: reproduced in under a second with 0049 + SLAM + constellation ALONE, no app, no client connected, plus a plausible code-confirmed mechanism (SCHED_FIFO max-priority preemption churn from 0049's own backoff sleep)
driver: Continuation of T193's fresh 0049 arm. Mid-session, user reported live, felt symptoms matching a pose-rate collapse ('un RE drift, muy notorio... cada 1 segundo shift de varios metros. Me fui del mapa') while Aircar was running; checked tracking.csv immediately and confirmed the collapse had started only 8.3s after monado-service's own startup (not at T192's 6m55s) -- a dramatically different, much faster onset than T192's original observation, with the identical downstream signature (~632-666ms locked pose interval). Aircar then crashed independently (real UE4 EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION at address 0x38 in the rendering thread, confirmed via a saved UE4Minidump.dmp and Proton's WINEDEBUG seh trace -- unrelated to Monado/0049, not investigated further). To isolate the collapse from any app-layer variable entirely, killed monado-service and relaunched clean with 0049, SLAM+constellation (WMR_CONSTELLATION_CONTROLLERS=1), and deliberately launched NO OpenXR client at all -- watched the fresh tracking.csv directly from its first samples.
veredicto:
MINIMAL REPRO, no app needed: pose interval was healthy (~37-86ms) for only the first ~6 samples, then collapsed to the same ~400-650ms signature at sample 7 -- roughly 0.3-0.5 seconds after monado-service started producing poses at all. NEW DETAIL not seen in T192/T193: the collapse is not perfectly monotonic on entry -- it recovered briefly (samples 24-30, back to ~16-99ms) before locking into the slow state again at sample 31 and staying there for the rest of the session (250+ samples, several minutes, still collapsed at last check). This oscillate-then-lock pattern is new information and points at a threshold-crossing mechanism rather than a one-way trigger.

THIS DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS T190's own pre-0049 measurement, which found SLAM+constellation alone idled cleanly with no sign of climbing over 1-2 minutes. The same subsystem combination, on the SAME hardware, now collapses in under a second once 0049 is in the binary -- about as clean and stark a before/after signal as this project has ever produced. Combined with T193's result (0/1 valid pre-0049 run, 45m47s with real load, never collapsed) this is now very strong evidence that 0049 -- not SLAM, not constellation, not the app, not CPU saturation (monado-service's own CPU was measured at only 59.1% during this minimal no-app repro, far below the 400-550% seen with an app running) -- is the actual trigger.

A CONCRETE, CODE-CONFIRMED MECHANISM HYPOTHESIS (not yet proven, but grounded in reading the actual source, not speculation): `wmr_run_thread` (the thread running both `control_read_packets` and `hololens_sensors_read_packets`) calls `u_linux_try_to_set_realtime_priority_on_thread()` at startup, which sets `SCHED_FIFO` at `sched_get_priority_max(SCHED_FIFO)` -- Linux's absolute maximum real-time priority (`u_linux.c`, confirmed by reading `pthread_setschedparam(this_thread, SCHED_FIFO, &params)` with `params.sched_priority = sched_get_priority_max(SCHED_FIFO)`). BEFORE 0049: on a failing companion read, the thread looped back immediately with no sleep -- under a sustained dropout this produced a tight busy-spin (T183/T188's measured 400%+ CPU, one thread pinned 99%+), monopolizing ONE core but not necessarily disturbing OTHER cores' scheduling. AFTER 0049: the thread now sleeps 10ms on every failing companion read once past the 50-consecutive threshold (which the universal storm crosses almost immediately) -- so instead of monopolizing one core continuously, it now wakes up roughly every 10ms (~100 times/second) and, because it holds the OS's maximum SCHED_FIFO priority, INSTANTLY PREEMPTS whatever normal-priority thread (SCHED_OTHER, which is almost certainly what Basalt's own worker threads run as) happens to be running on whatever core the scheduler places it on. This trades 'one core permanently wasted, contained' for 'a system-wide ~100Hz maximum-priority preemption pulse, uncontained' -- which is a very plausible way to wreck a tightly-timed VIO pipeline (Basalt) without the offending thread's OWN CPU% or the companion-read loop's OWN rate (independently measured healthy at ~100-105Hz in T192) ever looking abnormal. This also cleanly explains why T192's original code-level check (loop rate healthy) failed to find the mechanism: it was looking at the WRONG thread's throughput, not at what that thread's wakeups do to everyone else.

NOT YET DONE: this mechanism is a strong, code-grounded hypothesis, not a proven root cause -- it has not been directly instrumented (e.g. with a scheduler trace / perf sched, or by testing a fix that drops the thread out of SCHED_FIFO before sleeping and confirming the collapse stops). The obvious candidate fix, NOT implemented tonight: don't hold max SCHED_FIFO priority through the punitive backoff sleep -- e.g., temporarily drop scheduling class/priority before `os_nanosleep`, or lower the requested priority in the first place now that the thread is known to sleep routinely under a sustained (universal, expected) companion dropout.

modo: T195: LAB (Linux) -- perf sched trace during a live SLAM collapse, real scheduling data instead of hypotheses; DEFINITIVELY rules out CPU scheduling/preemption as the mechanism, narrowing the search to something logical inside the code (a lock/queue/timeout), not a scheduler problem
driver: Continuation of T194. First test: disabled SCHED_FIFO max priority specifically for wmr_hmd.c's read thread (new env-gated patch on top of 0049, WMR_HMD_THREAD_NO_RT=1 -- getenv() check added around u_linux_try_to_set_realtime_priority_on_thread(), rebuilt into the SAME binary as pure 0049 when the env var is unset, so this build stays behavior-identical to plain 0049 by default). Then, to get real scheduler data instead of more blind hypotheses: enabled perf's tracefs access (needed two rounds of sudo chmod from the user -- kernel.perf_event_paranoid=-1 and, after the first attempt at 'perf sched latency'/'perf script' failed with 'incompatible file format' even on freshly-recorded small traces, a broader `chmod -R o+rX /sys/kernel/tracing` beyond just its events/ subtree, which is what actually fixed it -- printk_formats and other sibling files under /sys/kernel/tracing/ were still root-only after the first, narrower chmod). Ran `perf sched record -a` (system-wide) across two full monado-service launches while the collapse happened, then `perf sched latency` on the resulting traces.
veredicto:
TEST 1 (RT priority disabled on the WMR read thread, sleep still present): DID NOT PREVENT THE COLLAPSE. Confirmed via /proc/<pid>/task and `ps -eLo pri,rtprio` that WMR: USB-HMD genuinely dropped to normal scheduling (pri=19, no rtprio) while another, unrelated monado-service thread (almost certainly the compositor's own frame-pacing thread) kept SCHED_FIFO 99 as expected -- so the experiment was real, not a no-op. The collapse still happened (onset at sample 9 this run, ~before its own consecutive-error backoff would have engaged much). This DIRECTLY DISPROVES T194's own leading hypothesis (SCHED_FIFO-max-priority preemption churn from the 10ms backoff sleep) -- ruled out, not confirmed. Left as a permanent, disabled-by-default WMR_HMD_THREAD_NO_RT=1 env-gate on top of 0049 in the current lab binary, documented here rather than reverted, in case it's useful again.

TEST 2 (perf sched trace, real launch, collapsed at sample 172 of that run -- yet another different onset timing, this time much later, joining T192's 6m55s, T194's 0.3s and 8.3s as a FOURTH distinct onset time observed across five total 0049 runs tonight -- the onset delay itself appears to have no fixed characteristic timescale, which is itself worth remembering): `perf sched latency -i` on the ~15-20s trace spanning the transition showed `WMR: USB-HMD`'s own max scheduling delay at 27.921ms runtime / 1121 switches / avg 0.005ms / MAX 0.026ms -- essentially instantaneous, textbook well-scheduled behavior, nowhere close to causing a 632ms-scale stall. The rest of monado-service's threads (aggregated by perf as 29 threads under the generic 'monado-service' comm, since most weren't individually named) showed avg delay 0.014ms, max delay 4.004ms, and 9230ms of actual RUNTIME across the ~15s window (over 60% average utilization) -- i.e. these threads were NOT starved of CPU time, they were running plenty, they just weren't successfully producing SLAM poses during it.

TEST 3 (perf sched trace, a THIRD fresh launch, this one never producing a single healthy pose at all -- tracking.csv stayed at 0 lines through the entire 15s trace despite gyro_bias_auto lines confirming the IMU pipeline was alive and processing): same clean result, WMR: USB-HMD max delay 0.026ms, aggregate monado-service threads max delay 4.004ms. The single worst-case scheduling delay found ANYWHERE in either trace, across every process on the whole system (not just monado-service), was still only in the hundreds-of-ms range for unrelated desktop processes (udev-worker, kdevtmpfs) doing their own unrelated work at trace start -- nothing remotely close to explaining a REPEATING ~632-666ms stall specifically tied to monado-service's pose pipeline.

CONCLUSION, stated plainly: scheduling/preemption/CPU-starvation, in any form (RT priority interaction, generic contention, thread starvation), is now RULED OUT by direct measurement, not just reasoned around. The threads involved are being scheduled promptly and are actively running; whatever is stalling pose production is a LOGICAL blocking mechanism inside the code itself -- a lock held across a long operation, a condition-variable wait not being signaled, a queue/buffer policy rejecting or delaying data, or a timestamp-validation path in Basalt's own VIO pipeline (t_tracker_slam.cpp on the Monado side, or inside Basalt's own separate upstream source, neither examined yet at this level of detail) getting stuck in a state that resolves only after a fixed multiple of some other period. The ~632-666ms figure itself, and its narrow (~1%) jitter across multiple independent runs and even multiple SEPARATE monado-service processes tonight, remains unexplained and is the strongest remaining clue -- it looks like a real code-level period (a timeout, a retry interval, a fixed sleep elsewhere), not organic system noise.

TOOLING NOTE for future perf use on this lab box: `sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=-1` alone is NOT sufficient for `perf sched record`/`latency`/`script` to work end-to-end as a non-root user -- tracefs (`/sys/kernel/tracing/`) also needs broadened read access, and it must be the WHOLE tree (`chmod -R o+rX /sys/kernel/tracing`), not just the `events/` subdirectory -- sibling files like `printk_formats` and `per_cpu/*` are read at record AND analysis time and their permissions get baked into whether the resulting perf.data file is even parseable later ('incompatible file format' on read-back was the actual symptom of an incomplete write-time permission set, not a corrupt-file or version-mismatch problem as first suspected).

modo: T197: LAB (Linux) -- first wearer session on the fixed stack: head latency is a CONSTANT ~1 s (smooth, no stutters, from the first movement, does not drain at rest); three levers tried live (vision-queue policy, constellation budget, SLAM threads) and none moved it more than marginally; drop-oldest on the OF->VIO queue is a measured NEGATIVE result
driver: Wearer protocol on the 360 test photo (dev 1 6dof + constellation, both controllers). Reports, in order: controllers initially absent then appearing ('parece todo 3dof' -> 'aparecieron'), later 'aparecen por unos segundos... con frames perdidos, muy cortado', head 'entre que muevo la cabeza y eso se refleja pasa facil un segundo'. Instruments: VIT_COLLAPSE_LOG IN/OUT t_ns deltas (pipeline debt), per-thread ps/gdb stack sampling (docs/42's poor-man's profiler), pose-lag.py cross-correlation, live A/Bs across 5 service cycles: (a) basalt 0009 (vision_data_queue capacity 10 -> 2 + drop-oldest push, mirroring 0001/0002); (b) WMR_CONSTELLATION_SEARCH_BUDGET_US=3000 (0051's lab test that docs/40 asked for); (c) 0009 corrected to blocking push (0010) after measurement; (d) SLAM_THREADS=4.
veredicto: THE FELT LAG IS CONSTANT-LATENCY, NOT RATE: 'muy claro y sin cortes, pero con delay constante de aprox 1 segundo', first movement included, still or moving -- the single most useful wearer characterization of the night. MEASURED CHAIN: pipeline debt (newest IN frame stamp minus newest OUT pose stamp) starts 133 ms and locks at ~632 ms; backend service time is ~63-66 ms/frame at rest but 133-400 ms/frame under real head motion, so arrival rate >= service rate ALWAYS and every bounded queue sits permanently full -- the debt is the steady state, it never drains (matches wearer: delay identical at rest). NEGATIVE RESULT, measured same night: 0009's drop-oldest made it WORSE -- the backend then only sees the newest survivor ~400 ms apart, every frame crosses the keyframe threshold, per-frame cost explodes 66->~400 ms (self-reinforcing ratchet to 2.5 Hz output = the OLD collapse signature reborn); corrected in 0010 to blocking push into the capacity-2 queue (backpressure moves shedding to the input side where 0002 already runs a tolerable equilibrium), backend back to 66-72 ms at rest. CONSTELLATION BUDGET LAB A/B: 3 ms cuts CPU 487->355% but kills matches exactly as on the everyday box -- controllers went from intermittent to parked at the shared placeholder ('anclados en 3dof en el mismo punto de partida... en el aire en un lugar random'), gdb stacks confirmed the no-budget burn is project_led_points/find_best_matching_led with num_blobs=29 -- so blob swamping is NOT everyday-box-specific; docs/40's refined direction (blob-count guard / controller-present gate) stands as the real path. SLAM_THREADS=4: no help (debt 699 ms, gaps erratic 34-266 ms) -- the wall is per-frame backend cost under motion, not thread count. pose-lag.py: delivered lags raw SLAM content by only +80 ms and filtering->prediction is +0.0 ms/0.00% residual -- prediction contributes NOTHING, which is what pointed at the delivery path and set up T198.

modo: T198: LAB (Linux) -- ROOT CAUSE PROVEN for the 632-666 ms magic number AND the constant ~1 s wearer lag: the camera frame timestamps run p50 +578 ms (max 610) IN THE FUTURE of the query/IMU clock -- a stable clock-domain-conversion bias that also explains docs/39's image-ahead-of-IMU stall; dead reckoning is healthy but integrates only the ~90 ms the lying stamps show it
driver: A sonnet agent read the whole prediction path (t_tracker_slam.cpp, t_dead_reckoning.c, m_predict.c, m_filter_fifo.c, wmr_hmd.c/wmr_source.c) and delivered: anchor = slam_rels.get_latest, IMU from gyro_ff/accel_ff (1000-entry count-bound rings), no horizon cap, and a no-partial-credit return-false fallback that silently delivers the bare stale anchor -- plus a free diagnostic: the failure paths log by default. Live grep: ZERO hits -- dead reckoning never fails. So a 12-line rate-limited INFO was added at the call site (monado 0052) printing the anchor age it actually sees, service cycled once (panel stayed dark -- companion re-enumerated after the service opened it, stale fd, known class), and the log then carried both the anchor ages and the newest camera-frame stamps interleaved within milliseconds of each other.

driver: Autonomous program (user resting, standing authorization). Ingest instrumentation first (monado 0053: per-frame raw cam-vs-IMU hw skew + converted-stamp-vs-now at receive_cam0, first 30 frames verbose then 1/300): a FRESH idle session started HONEST (skew -4..0ms, converted stamps -4.5ms past; frames 1-4 pre-first-IMU also exposed the raw device hw clock at +16.45s vs host) -- killing the 'constant bias' and 'startup burst' hypotheses in one capture. Then the same idle session RAMPED from -2.45ms to +630ms between frames ~300 and ~1200 (under 40s, no app, no wearer) and pinned there rock-stable -- a bounded buffer filling. hw2mono moved +630 in lockstep: the IMU stream itself had fallen ~630ms behind (stale hw stamps at arrival), and the offset estimator dutifully absorbed it. Mechanism identified in wmr_hmd.c: control_read_packets (companion) and hololens_sensors_read_packets share ONE sequential loop (T194); 0049's storm backoff was a 10ms os_nanosleep INSIDE that loop, capping hololens/IMU reads at ~100/s vs ~250 packets/s produced -- ring fills, lag pins at ring capacity (~630ms), onset whenever the storm crosses the 50-failure threshold (variable: explains T192-T195's 'no fixed timescale' onsets AND why the collapse appeared WITH 0049, never before it -- T193's pre-0049 run spun without pacing the loop). Windows RE cross-confirms the failure class: MRUSBHost.dll carries IMUStaleDataDrop / CameraReaderLoopRestartingIMU (Windows detects-and-restarts a stale IMU stream). Fix 0055: back off by SKIPPING companion attempts until companion_backoff_until_ns instead of sleeping -- same <=100Hz companion retry ceiling, zero loop-pace impact; WMR_COMPANION_BACKOFF_BLOCKING=1 restores old behavior for A/B.
veredicto: VALIDATED AT MECHANISM LEVEL, wearer verdict pending: 8-minute idle session with the storm ACTIVE the whole time (39792 companion errors, 39000+ consecutive -- the exact old trigger): cam-vs-IMU raw skew flat -4..-0.7ms across 14400 frames (old: +630 by frame 1200), converted camera stamps steady -4.5ms in the honest past, prediction anchor age now reads the TRUE content age (~144ms idle) so dead reckoning can finally bridge real staleness. Full causal chain, every mystery of the saga accounted for: 0049 sleep -> IMU ring fill (~630ms) -> hw2mono absorption -> camera stamps future -> (a) Basalt image-ahead-of-IMU stall = the collapse (0007/0008 remain as robustness), (b) stamps lie to prediction = the constant ~1s felt latency. PENDING, needs the user: wearer feel test (expected: head rotation immediate -- under load the real pipeline debt remains ~150-600ms but is now VISIBLE to prediction and gyro-bridged), controllers powered for a real session, and the >15min keepalive A/B. modo: T211: LAB (Linux) -- the HMD roll-drift debt (T162 -> T203's +0.9deg/min) gets its mechanism: chair-oscillation test proves a ~9pct yaw->roll/pitch cross-axis leak (~7.3deg gyro mounting misalignment), calibration-class, matrix-fixable; the gamer chair graduates as the headset's rotation fixture (turntable cannot bear its weight)
driver: Fixture decision forced by physics: the turntable does not withstand the headset's weight ('no resiste el peso del casco'), and single-direction rotation is banned by the tether (cable winds) -- the user's own proposal became the standard: headset on the PC chair, hand-oscillated side to side, wide amplitude. The discriminating design: OSCILLATION back and forth means a pure bias would cancel over reversals while a proportional cross-axis leak accumulates with |yaw traveled| regardless of direction. RESULT from the slam CSVs: roll and pitch error grow PROPORTIONAL to yaw traveled at ~+0.091 (roll) / -0.089 (pitch) -- i.e. ~9pct of every yaw degree leaks into roll/pitch, consistent with a ~7.3deg gyro mounting misalignment about a fixed axis. This RECONCILES the whole history: at rest the leak has nothing to amplify (T203's -0.027deg/min sign-flipping noise), worn it rides actual head yaw (T203's +0.84-0.93deg/min at R2=0.80 -- people yaw constantly, roll rarely), and it is NOT Basalt gyro-bias-under-dynamics (round 1 map item 2's hypothesis) but a static geometric calibration error upstream of everything. Matrix-fixable: agent tasked with fitting WMR_HMD_GYRO_MOUNT_FIX (env-gated, default off, composed into the gyro transform in wmr_hmd_get_imu_calib, gyro-only per 0065's accel lesson) from the leak coefficients; validation design = a second chair pass with the fix active should show leak ~0. Held-out validation planned: the follow-up quorum test (headset + both controllers rigid on one plane on the chair -- three gyros, one shared true motion, any disagreement is per-device calibration error) doubles as fit-validation data the fit never saw.
veredicto: The left-roll debt open since T162 finally has a mechanism, a number, and a fix path: ~9pct cross-axis leak from ~7.3deg of gyro mounting misalignment -- static, geometric, matrix-correctable; NOT bias estimation under dynamics. The chair-oscillation protocol joins the turntable and cradle in the calibration instrument catalog (weight class: headset; motion class: oscillation-only, tether-safe). Fit agent in flight as this entry opens; chair validation pass follows the fix.

modo: T212: LAB (Linux) -- the physical quorum test (three gyros, one rigid plane, one shared motion) and its two verdicts: the controllers vote UNANIMOUS (gain L/R 0.9905, axis wobble <1 deg both hands -- 0071 machine-confirmed in the wild), and the HMD 9pct-leak premise of T211 is REFUTED by held-out data before the fix was ever enabled; plus the mik cell field failure that validates the docs/46 cliff model, keepalive v2's first real evidence, and a USB2 full-death recovered

The already-built WMR_HMD_GYRO_MOUNT_FIX (0072, fitted by an agent that itself caught a naive axis-swap via three independent checks -- good method on a doomed premise) is shelved default-off as a documented negative result; pass 2 CANCELLED (enabling a 7.34 deg correction that does not exist would inject the leak). Blob-quality and 0056-guard levers: EXONERATED for this failure mode (a fresh MAX_BLOBS baseline is still worth capturing someday -- p90 reached 171/camera -- but nothing is blocked by it).
veredicto: The single most valuable capture of the controller era: one 20-min protocol converted 'hands park and nobody knows why' into a named, quantified, hand-asymmetric mechanism with a structural explanation for why every existing defense missed it (gravity-blind ghost lobe) -- and simultaneously explained the yaw-wind healer starvation (D) as the SAME mechanism. modo: T218: CORRECTION of T217 -- there is no 9ms pacer quantum: xrizer's GetFrameTiming returns a HARDCODED stub (m_flTotalRenderGpuMs=9.0) and the benchmark's 111.11 = 1000/9.0, pure fiction; the user's skepticism wins twice; the real fix is real frame-timing metrics in xrizer
driver: Third identical 111.11 run -- now WITH U_PACING_APP_IMMEDIATE_WAIT_FRAME_RETURN=1 (free-run) and scale 100 -- killed the pacer theory: two resolutions x two pacing modes, one number. Source dive found it: compositor.rs GetFrameTiming (the one implemented version, 028) fills the struct with constants -- PreSubmitGpu 8.0, PostSubmitGpu 1.0, TotalRenderGpu 9.0, CompositorRenderGpu 1.5, etc. The benchmark derives FPS from the timing struct: 1000/9.0 = 111.11 exactly, avg=lows because the 'measurement' never varies. T217's claims RETRACTED accordingly: no evidence of Monado over-granting frames, no measured 19pct discarded render, no 9ms wait_frame cadence -- the app loop rate was never actually measured (a Tracy trace can still do that someday, as a separate question with no current evidence of a problem). What SURVIVES from T217: scale-100 knob works; overlay-helper gap; prewarm first swap; launch-options recipe hardening. THE REAL FIX, named: implement genuine frame timing in xrizer -- fill Compositor_FrameTiming from measured values (frame index/time metrics infra partially exists at self.metrics; GPU ms needs real timestamps or at least honest CPU-side frame-delta) -- unlocking truthful benchmark scores, the Proton A/B, and the whole fpsVR instrument class. ALSO this run (wearer, in passing): noticeable head drift during the benchmark session (env had free-run + pipelined; possibly prediction under an unthrottled client, or plain SLAM after many session cycles -- observation only, benchmark ignores tracking).

'Es un chamullo' -- correct at every level. Fix queued: real FrameTiming in xrizer; until then NO OpenVR-side timing number from this stack is to be believed.
